text_blocks.snippet: A blood pressure reading below 90/60 mmHg is generally considered low (hypotension). While some people naturally have low blood pressure without experiencing any issues, a sudden drop or low readings accompanied by symptoms can indicate a problem.

list.snippet: Normal Blood Pressure: For most adults, a normal blood pressure reading is less than 120/80 mmHg.
Low Blood Pressure (Hypotension): A reading below 90/60 mmHg is generally considered low.
When to be concerned:
Low blood pressure with symptoms: Dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, blurred vision, nausea, or fatigue can be signs that your blood pressure is too low and may be affecting your body.
Sudden drops in blood pressure: A sudden drop in blood pressure can be dangerous, especially if it affects blood flow to vital organs like the brain.

Individual Differences: What's considered "too low" can vary from person to person. Some individuals may naturally have low blood pressure without any problems, while others may experience symptoms at similar readings.
Consult your doctor: If you have concerns about your blood pressure, it's best to consult with a healthcare professional for personalized advice.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, while a reading below 90/60 mmHg is often considered low, the significance of low blood pressure depends on individual factors and the presence of any associated symptoms.

related_questions.question: When should I go to the ER for low blood pressure?

text_blocks.snippet: Go to the ER for low blood pressure if you experience symptoms like dizziness, fainting, shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of shock (cold, clammy skin, rapid breathing, weak or rapid pulse, or bluish skin tone). Also, seek immediate medical attention if you have confusion, especially in older adults or those taking blood pressure medication, or if you have a suspected fracture after a fall.
snippet_highlighted_words: if you experience symptoms like dizziness, fainting, shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of shock (cold, clammy skin, rapid breathing, weak or rapid pulse, or bluish skin tone)

text_blocks.snippet: When to go to the ER:

list.title: Fainting or loss of consciousness:
list.snippet: If you or someone else passes out due to low blood pressure, seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Signs of shock:
list.snippet: These include cold and sweaty skin, rapid breathing, a blue skin tone, or a weak and rapid pulse.

list.title: Severe symptoms:
list.snippet: Dizziness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath, chest pain, or confusion, especially in older adults or those taking blood pressure medication, warrant immediate evaluation.

list.title: Suspected fracture:
list.snippet: If a fall results in a suspected fracture, seek emergency care.

list.title: Severe allergic reaction:
list.snippet: If low blood pressure is part of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) with symptoms like hives, swelling of the mouth, tongue, or throat, go to the ER.

list.title: Symptoms of stroke or heart attack:
list.snippet: If you have sudden weakness or numbness, trouble seeing, slurred speech, chest pain, or other stroke/heart attack symptoms, call 911 immediately.

list.title: Uncontrolled bleeding:
list.snippet: Any uncontrolled bleeding can cause dangerously low blood pressure and requires immediate medical attention.

list.title: Rapid, shallow breathing:
list.snippet: This can be a sign of serious complications like shock or respiratory distress.
If you have occasional but non-critical hypotensive symptoms (like lightheadedness) or if your home blood pressure readings are consistently below 90/60, contact your primary care provider.
If you have chronically low blood pressure and it causes symptoms like dizziness, fatigue, fainting, nausea, or difficulty concentrating, consult your doctor.

list.title: Individual variations:
list.snippet: Low blood pressure is defined as a reading below 90/60 mm Hg, but a reading this low isn't always a cause for concern if you have no symptoms.

list.title: Underlying conditions:
list.snippet: Low blood pressure can be a symptom of various conditions, some of which can be serious, so it's important to get evaluated if you experience symptoms.

related_questions.question: What is a critically low blood pressure?

text_blocks.snippet: Critical low blood pressure, also known as hypotension, is a dangerous condition where blood pressure drops to dangerously low levels, potentially causing organ damage due to insufficient blood flow and oxygen delivery. Readings below 90/60 mm Hg are generally considered hypotensive. If severe, it can lead to shock, a life-threatening condition where vital organs fail.
snippet_highlighted_words: a dangerous condition where blood pressure drops to dangerously low levels, potentially causing organ damage due to insufficient blood flow and oxygen delivery

list.snippet: Dizziness or lightheadedness: A common symptom as blood flow to the brain is reduced.
Fainting: Can occur due to a sudden drop in blood pressure.
Blurred or fading vision: Reduced blood flow can affect vision.
Fatigue and confusion: The brain needs adequate blood flow to function properly.
Nausea: May occur due to the body's response to low blood pressure.
Cold, clammy skin: A sign of reduced blood flow to the skin.
Rapid, shallow breathing: The body may try to compensate for reduced oxygen.
Rapid, weak pulse: The heart may beat faster to try to pump more blood.
Bluish skin tone (cyanosis): A sign of severe oxygen deprivation.
Shock: Extreme low blood pressure can lead to shock, a life-threatening condition.
Severe bleeding: Internal or external blood loss can significantly lower blood pressure.
Infections (sepsis): Severe infections can trigger a systemic inflammatory response, leading to dangerously low blood pressure.
Anaphylaxis: A severe allergic reaction can cause a rapid drop in blood pressure.
Heart conditions: Heart attacks, arrhythmias, and other heart problems can impair the heart's ability to pump blood effectively.
Dehydration: Reduces blood volume and can lead to low blood pressure.
Medications: Certain medications, like those for high blood pressure, can lower blood pressure.
Pregnancy: Blood pressure tends to drop during pregnancy.
Nervous system disorders: Conditions like Parkinson's disease can affect blood pressure regulation.
Endocrine disorders: Addison's disease, where the adrenal glands don't produce enough hormones, can lead to hypotension.

text_blocks.snippet: When to Seek Immediate Medical Attention:

list.snippet: Sudden, severe drop in blood pressure: Especially if accompanied by other symptoms.
Signs of shock: Cold, clammy skin, rapid breathing, weak pulse, bluish skin tone.
Loss of consciousness: If someone faints or becomes unresponsive, seek immediate medical help.
Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis): Seek immediate medical attention.
Treating underlying causes: Addressing the root cause of the hypotension is crucial.
Medications: Medications to raise blood pressure and improve heart function may be necessary.
Fluids: Intravenous fluids (IV) can help restore blood volume.
Blood transfusion: If blood loss is the cause, blood transfusion may be needed.
Addressing shock: Shock requires immediate medical intervention, including medications and supportive care.
Compression stockings: Can help improve blood flow from the legs.
Lifestyle changes: May include drinking more fluids, increasing salt intake (with medical advice), and avoiding prolonged standing.

text_blocks.snippet: Low blood pressure, also known as hypotension, is generally considered dangerous when it falls below 90/60 mmHg (millimeters of mercury). This means that the systolic pressure (top number) is less than 90 mmHg and the diastolic pressure (bottom number) is less than 60 mmHg.

Extremely low blood pressure, defined as a systolic pressure below 60 mmHg or a diastolic pressure below 40 mmHg, can be life-threatening. It can lead to inadequate blood flow to vital organs such as the brain, heart, and kidneys, resulting in symptoms such as:

list.snippet: Dizziness
Fainting
Confusion
Nausea
Cold, clammy skin
Rapid heart rate

text_blocks.snippet: If you experience a sudden drop in blood pressure or have persistent low blood pressure accompanied by symptoms, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention. Low blood pressure can be a sign of an underlying medical condition that requires treatment.
